newsitem.title: USA: Aberdeen commander retires early, admits adultery.
newsitem.headline: Aberdeen commander retires early, admits adultery.

text.p: The commander of the U.S. Army's scandal-plagued Aberdeen Proving Ground is to retire after admitting to an adulterous affair more than five years ago, officials said on Tuesday.

Maj. Gen. John Longhouser, a West Point graduate and decorated 32-year veteran, said he was retiring in view of a relationship he had had with a civilian while he was in divorce proceedings, although he eventually reconciled with his wife.

"In view of this past relationship and the concern currently being focused on the military and the personal lives of its members, my family and I have decided that it would be best for me to retire at this time," Longhouser said in a statement.
A Pentagon official earlier confirmed a New York Times report that Longhouser, 53, had admitted to an adulterous affair.
Longhouser's early retirement is the latest incident as military scrutiny implicates top officers and enlisted soldiers in allegations of sexual harassment or marital cheating.

"We have very high standards that we insist upon for the military ... It's another example of someone who failed to measure up to those standards," Defence Secretary William Cohen said at a joint news conference with visiting British Defence Secretary George Robertson.

Calling the case "unfortunate," Cohen said Longhouser himself decided that he was "in a compromising position" because he was the man who decided when others might face military trials for sex-related offences.
The proving ground is the site of a major sexual misconduct scandal in which 12 trainers at the base's Ordnance Centre and School have been charged with preying on female trainees.

Longhouser, who also was serving as commander of the Army's Test and Evaluation Command, was not directly responsible for the school, which was part of a separate military unit. But he was responsible for convening courts martial on base.
Longhouser stepped down from his posts Tuesday although his retirement takes effect on June 30, proving ground spokesman John Yaquiant said.

A Pentagon official said Longhouser, a two-star general, will retire at the rank of a one-star general, which will mean a reduction by about $10,000 a year in his retirement benefits. He will not have served long enough as a two-star general to qualify for the benefits.

The New York Times said in a report the military had received an anonymous tip about Longhouser over a telephone hot line established to field calls after revelations of the sexual misconduct scandal at Aberdeen.

Longhouser said in the statement he had reconciled with his wife, Karen, and informed her of the relationship. "Today, our marriage is as strong as ever, and Karen is my best friend as well as a loving and loyal wife," he said.

"I am sorry for any pain or embarrassment I have brought to my family ...," he said. He added, "I feel I have made contributions to the Army and hope it is for those contributions that people remember me."
Defence Secretary Cohen said high-level cases of sexual misconduct in the U.S. military were not "epidemic" and praised the armed forces for dealing with the matter openly.
"I think we're going through a period in which this has become very much in high profile," he said in response to reporters' questions at the Pentagon.
"I believe overall our military is doing an outstanding job; our leaders are doing an outstanding job and we are dealing with the issue in a very proactive and open fashion."

Of the 12 Ordnance Centre and School trainers charged in a sexual misconduct investigation disclosed last November, four were found guilty of violations, two received discharges in lieu of court-martial and six are awaiting resolution.
Longhouser will be replaced on a temporary basis by Maj. Gen. George Friel, commander of the Army's Chemical and Biological Defence Command.
